title: Review gate: Claude Opus review + independent OpenAI (codex) review, fix loop, both must PASS
question:
GUEST MESSAGING REVIEW GATE (tree-6afc7590 node #1705) — both reviewers agree on every fact; one item left is a product call only you can make.

BOTH VERDICTS: FAIL, on this single open item. reviews/guest-messages-opus.md and reviews/guest-messages-openai.md are committed on feat/guest-messages (nothing merged; main is still at rehearsal-1). 7 of 8 findings are fixed across commits 9d12f74, 9efdb2f, e9137a5, f848d0d. No test file was touched and no suite was run.

THE OPEN ITEM: a send that fails at the same moment a booking is cancelled can still message the cancelled guest. Only reachable if the send throws — in this branch 'sending' is a Log::info, so it is effectively unreachable today, but it is a real hole and three successive fixes failed to close it. The reason is structural, not a coding slip: 'pending' has to mean both 'the dispatcher may send this' AND 'a cancellation may still skip this'. The cancellation sweep and the per-minute dispatcher both key on exactly that state and nothing orders them, so any release that puts the row back to pending can be claimed by another worker before the cancellation is noticed. (Full interleaving: Pass 5 of the OpenAI review.)

TWO WAYS OUT — each trades one guest-visible failure for another:

(A) DROP THE RELEASE. Claim-then-send, and a send that fails leaves the row claimed and undelivered, logged at error level. The race disappears completely and this is exactly what the written Rule 7 tests describe. Cost: a failed send silently loses a guest's check-in message, permanently — in a feature whose whole point is that guests get their messages automatically. Both reviewers flagged that loss as blocking on the first pass.

(B) ADD AN IN-FLIGHT STATE ('sending'), so a released row is never momentarily dispatchable, plus recovery for abandoned claims — a worker killed mid-send strands the row in 'sending' forever otherwise. This is the correct long-term design and is compatible with the written tests (they only assert the state handle() ENDS in). Cost: the recovery needs a reclaim timeout — 'after N minutes assume the worker died and re-queue' — which deliberately weakens 'a guest never gets the same message twice', because a merely slow worker would then send twice. It also needs a call on what /messages shows a host for a mid-flight message.

QUESTION: (A) lose a message on send failure, or (B) risk a duplicate on a slow worker? If (B): what reclaim timeout, and should an in-flight message show to the host as 'Upcoming' or as its own state? Either way the follow-up is small and self-contained in app/Jobs/SendGuestMessage.php.

My recommendation: (B) with a deliberately long reclaim window (e.g. 15 min) — a duplicate check-in message is an apology, a missing one is a guest locked out. But it only starts mattering once a real sender replaces the Log::info, so (A) plus a loud alert is a defensible way to ship rehearsal 1 today and decide (B) when the sender lands.

REAL BUGS THE GATE CAUGHT AND FIXED (both reviewers found the top two independently):
1. Property::localInstant() parsed with 'Y-m-d H:i', which leaves seconds/microseconds unspecified, so PHP filled them from the live clock. Carbon rebases the parse on the mock under a frozen clock, so EVERY send_at assertion passed while production would store 21:00:37 — messages up to a minute late, non-deterministic send times, wrong-looking times for the host. The tests structurally could not catch it. Fixed with startOfMinute().
2. ReservationObserver only observed created(), so cancelling a reservation never reached the planner: a cancelled guest still got check-in instructions. BOTH cancellation tests hid this by calling scheduleFor() directly after saving. Fixed by adding updated().
3. SendGuestMessage claimed the row before sending, so a send that threw left it 'sent' and undelivered with every retry no-opping. Fixed (and is what opened the open item above).
4. Existing reservations predating the feature had no messages and nothing called scheduleAll(). Wired as 'messages:plan-all', an idempotent backfill.
5. Planner re-ran MessageTemplate::all() and the property lookup per reservation, and did two SELECTs per template. Fixed.
6. scheduled_messages indexed send_at alone while the per-minute query is status + send_at. Replaced with a composite.
7. The new Reservation::property() relation collided with the 'property' column — Eloquent resolves the attribute first, so an eager-loaded relation would be silently unreachable. Renamed propertyRecord().
8. My own fix for #5 removed Laravel 13's unique-violation recovery (updateOrCreate goes through createOrFirst, Builder.php:771), so a concurrent observer and backfill could blow up on the unique index. Caught by the OpenAI review, not by me. Fixed with createOrFirst().

VERIFIED BY READING, NOT RUNNING: the 24-absolute-hour DST maths is correct (2026-11-01 15:00 Chicago CST = 21:00 UTC, minus 24h = 2026-10-31 21:00 UTC = 16:00 CDT); the idempotency IS a genuine row-level claim (a true concurrent double-dispatch cannot send twice — the second UPDATE re-evaluates status='pending' against the committed row and matches zero); migrations are sound (the unique(reservation_id, message_template_id) is what makes the tests' sole() calls real); CarbonImmutable::setTestNow() does reach now() and Date::now() in Carbon 3 via the single FactoryImmutable. All 16 test methods would pass as written and every fix was chosen to keep them true.

TESTS FOR KEVIN (not written — I cannot run anything to confirm they pass): nothing pins the scheduler wiring (that routes/console.php registers messages:dispatch-due on everyMinute()->withoutOverlapping()); nothing pins the new updated() observer or messages:plan-all; and the 'concurrent' idempotency test is sequential (it pre-marks the row sent) so it exercises the predicate, not two simultaneous claims, and nothing covers the failed-send release path.
why: Worker stated its own recommendation ('My recommendation: (B) with a deliberately long reclaim window ...'), so the steward can auto-answer instead of parking.
